extracted.intended_audience: law students, academics, patent practitioners, and policymakers interested in Indian patent law (esp. pharmaceuticals)
extracted.subtask_description: Critical legal analysis of Section 3(d) of the Indian Patents Act, 1970 addressing when new forms/derivatives of known substances are patentable, how 'efficacy' is interpreted (esp. for medicines), and related case law and policy implications.

rubrics_metrics.name: Section 3(d) prohibition on patenting mere discovery
rubrics_metrics.description: Section 3(d): 'The mere discovery of a new form of a known substance which does not result in increased efficacy of that substance or the mere discovery of any new property or new use for a known substance or of the mere use of a known process, machine or apparatus unless such process results in a new product or employs at least one new reactant' is not patentable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The provision bars patenting of mere discoveries and minor modifications unless they meet the increased-efficacy (or other stated) exceptions; the article frames S.3(d) as targeted to prevent 'evergreening'.

rubrics_metrics.name: Explanation: categories treated as the same substance
rubrics_metrics.description: The Explanation to S.3(d) lists salts, esters, ethers, polymorphs, metabolites, pure form, particle size, isomers, mixtures of isomers, complexes, combinations and other derivatives of a known substance as being considered the same substance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These derivatives are treated as the same substance 'unless they differ significantly in properties with regard to efficacy.' Use this list to identify when a claimed 'new form' is actually the 'same substance' under S.3(d).

rubrics_metrics.name: Three-condition framework for S.3(d) applicability
rubrics_metrics.description: From the section's wording, three conditions must be satisfied for S.3(d) to apply: (1) what is claimed must be a 'mere discovery'; (2) it must be a new form of a known substance; and (3) such claimed substance does not bring about increased efficacy over the known substance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If any of the three conditions are not met, S.3(d) should not apply. Use these sequentially to assess whether S.3(d) bars patentability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mere discovery vs invention (definition and test)
rubrics_metrics.description: 'Discovery' is used in its ordinary English sense (Webster): the act or instance of gaining knowledge of something previously unrecognized; i.e., something that existed in nature but was previously unknown. By contrast, inventions involving substantive human intervention (e.g., lab-designed biological constructs via recombinant DNA) are not mere discoveries.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply this to distinguish naturally pre-existing items (likely 'discoveries') from human-made or substantially modified items (likely 'inventions'). Example: paracetamol having a newly-identified property (pain-relieving) would be a discovery and not patentable under S.3(d).

rubrics_metrics.name: New form of a known substance — scope and limits
rubrics_metrics.description: S.3(d) targets 'new forms' (derivatives) of known chemical substances; the Explanation’s expansive language covers many possible derivatives but qualifies them by the need to 'differ significantly in properties as to efficacy' to be patentable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: a new use of aspirin (cardiovascular) that is merely a new use of a known substance is not patentable, whereas a new and alternative process for preparing aspirin may be patentable as a process invention.

rubrics_metrics.name: Enhanced efficacy requirement (threshold for patentability)
rubrics_metrics.description: New forms of known substances are unpatentable under S.3(d) unless they demonstrate 'increased efficacy'—the statute and explanation require a meaningful/substantial increase, not a trivial or minor improvement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The article emphasizes that the improvement must be 'significant' in efficacy rather than a trifling increase; courts have required a clear, demonstrable enhancement (see cases cited). Use this as a high substantive threshold when evaluating pharmaceutical derivatives.

rubrics_metrics.name: Efficacy meaning in judicial interpretation (Novartis precedent)
rubrics_metrics.description: The Supreme Court (in Novartis) interpreted 'efficacy' as 'ability to produce the desired or intended result' and held that for medicines the relevant test is 'therapeutic efficacy'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply therapeutic efficacy as the metric when assessing pharmaceutical patent claims under S.3(d). Example: Novartis' imatinib mesylate (beta-crystalline polymorph B) failed because it did not show enhanced therapeutic efficacy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Process/use exception: when mere use of known process is patentable
rubrics_metrics.description: S.3(d) excludes patentability of 'the mere use of a known process, machine or apparatus' unless such process results in a new product or employs at least one new reactant.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess process claims to see whether they produce a new product or involve a new reactant; if so, S.3(d) will not bar patentability of the process-related subject-matter.

rubrics_metrics.name: Derivative differs 'significantly in properties with regard to efficacy' (exception test)
rubrics_metrics.description: Derivatives/variants (salts, polymorphs, isomers, particle size changes, etc.) are treated as the same substance unless they differ significantly in efficacy properties; only then can they escape S.3(d)'s bar.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evidence must show significant property differences in efficacy; mere structural or minor physicochemical differences are insufficient without corresponding efficacy gains.

rubrics_metrics.name: Judicial standard on mere workshop improvements and inventive step
rubrics_metrics.description: Biswanath Prasad Radhe Shyam v. Hindustan Metal Industries establishes that an improvement must be more than a mere workshop improvement; it must satisfy the test of invention/inventive step and produce a new result.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use this judicial test to reject patents that are only trivial modifications lacking inventive step; the improvement must contribute a non-obvious, functional advance.

rubrics_metrics.name: TRIPS baseline patentability requirements and member-state flexibilities
rubrics_metrics.description: TRIPS sets baseline requirements (novelty, inventive step, industrial application). Member states may adopt more stringent criteria; Article 27.1 does not define 'invention' or 'inventive step', allowing national discretion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Section 3(d)'s higher threshold (enhanced efficacy requirement) can be consistent with TRIPS because TRIPS allows countries flexibility to set standards of patentability aligned with social/economic needs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Comparative U.S. approach to patenting improvements (35 U.S.C. §101)
rubrics_metrics.description: U.S. law (35 U.S.C. §101) permits patents on 'any new and useful improvement' of a process, machine, manufacture, or composition; the U.S. provides procedural vehicles (continuation, divisional, continuation-in-part) and typically a lower threshold for 'improvements' than S.3(d).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When analyzing policy impacts or comparing systems, note that the U.S. is more permissive toward incremental improvements, which contrasts with India's stricter S.3(d) stance aimed at preventing evergreening.

rubrics_metrics.name: Policy objective: preventing 'evergreening' and protecting public health
rubrics_metrics.description: S.3(d) was introduced to prevent 'evergreening'—patenting of insignificant modifications of existing patented inventions—to avoid undue extension of monopolies and to protect access to affordable generics and public health.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Policy justifications (FICCI roundtable, WHO commentary) support S.3(d) as a public-interest measure; evidence cited includes patent-grant statistics and the Novartis outcome as safeguarding access to medicines.

rubrics_metrics.name: Critique: vagueness and administrative discretion regarding 'efficacy'
rubrics_metrics.description: The article criticizes S.3(d) for not clearly defining 'enhanced efficacy' or providing guidelines, thereby leaving wide discretionary power to the Controller and creating uncertainty.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recommendation: clarify or amend the wording of S.3(d) to define 'enhanced efficacy' and set standards/guidelines for assessment to reduce perceived arbitrariness.
